steps.client: The design is ready. Nothing is printed yet.
steps.pm: Design freeze (G3) and crew booked for three build days.
steps.expert: Twin v4 sliced into 72 layers; each fits one 202 mL cartridge.

steps.t: Dry run: drones fly the path with lights
steps.client: Test flight done. Printing can start.
steps.expert: Tracking within tolerance; wind limit set to 6 m/s.

steps.pm: Two drones alternating; refill after every layer.
steps.expert: Every layer scanned; deviations under 5 mm.

steps.client: A shape issue was found and the design adjusted. Still on track.
steps.pm: Design change approved; no schedule impact.
steps.expert: Three layers out of tolerance; offsets didn't fix it. Layers 19–72 revised to v5, stability checked.

steps.client: Paused for wind. 22 of 72 layers done.
steps.pm: Hold passed the mix's open time: one cartridge discarded.
steps.expert: Gusts 6.9 m/s over the 6 m/s limit. Resumed after 50 min.

steps.client: One drone is out for the day. Work continues.
steps.pm: Slower: one drone, refilling between every layer.
steps.expert: Remaining layers reassigned to BuilDrone 1 within open time.

steps.t: Day 3: cold morning, cure wait at layer 41
steps.client: Short wait this morning for the material to set.
steps.pm: Backup refill technician called in; start 30 min late.
steps.expert: 6 °C: layer 40 needs ~22 min before it can carry layer 41.

steps.client: Finished and accepted, with notes on layers 16–18.
steps.pm: Acceptance gate (G5) passed; decision log archived.
steps.expert: Laser scan median 2.6 mm; local exceedance at 16–18 absorbed by v5.

stages.title: Brief and site
stages.what: Goal, size, height, access, site conditions
questions: What are we building, and what is it for?
How big and how high is it, and where?
Can a crane, gantry or ground robot reach the whole build?
What does success look like, and by when?

stages.title: Fabrication method
stages.what: Aerial AM or a ground method
questions: Does size, access, congestion or scaffolding justify drones?
What would a ground method cost and take instead?
Is the team willing to carry the extra risk of a new method?

stages.title: Geometry
questions: Does the form slice into horizontal layers?
Are walls thin enough, and overhangs supported?
Which parts are inclined, and how steep?

stages.title: Material and tests
stages.what: Mix trials: weight, flow, shape, curing
questions: Foam or cement, and which mix?
Does it hold shape under downwash and the next layers?
How long does it stay workable, and how fast does it set?
Does it fit the payload per trip?

stages.title: Role and tolerance
questions: Is it enclosure, formwork, insulation or repair?
What deviation is acceptable for this role?
Does it need reinforcement or code approval?

stages.title: Digital twin and toolpath
questions: Does every interim stage stand on the twin?
Which toolpath gives the fewest trips?
Where would we redesign, re-sequence or scaffold?

stages.title: Plan and budget
questions: How many layers and trips, and how long?
How many robots, and how many crew per shift?
What is the budget for material, robots and crew?
Which permits and airspace approvals do we need?
What is frozen now, and what can still change?

stages.title: Site setup
stages.what: Positioning, refill station, safety zone, weather
questions: How do robots know where they are on this site?
Where is the refill and battery station?
Where is the safety zone, and who guards it?
How do we measure wind and temperature?

stages.title: Dry run
stages.what: Light-trace flight of the path, no material
questions: Do the robots follow the path within tolerance?
Do they keep safe spacing at the tightest layer?
Is the team ready to start printing?

stages.title: Load
stages.what: Material and battery onto the drone
questions: Is the mix still within its open time?
Is the battery enough for this layer?

stages.title: Deposit
questions: Is the robot tracking the path?
Is the flow matching the flight speed?

stages.title: Scan
stages.what: Camera drone maps the new layer
questions: Is the scan complete, with no gaps?

stages.title: Evaluate
questions: Is the layer within tolerance?
Has the layer below cured enough?
Does the next stage stay stable?
Are wind and temperature within limits?

stages.title: Adapt
stages.what: Offset the next path or redesign
questions: Can an offset fix the drift?
Is the drift large enough to redesign upper layers?
Has the change been logged as a new version?

stages.title: Layer gate
questions: Go, hold or adjust for the next layer?
If a robot failed: reassign or stop at this layer?
Who decided, and on what evidence?

stages.title: Final validation
questions: Does the as-built match the design within tolerance?
Accept, accept with notes, or remediate?

stages.title: Handover
questions: What did we learn about limits, mixes and weather?
What goes into the next project's defaults?
Is every decision traceable to its evidence?

decisions.title: Fabrication method
decisions.question: Which process can build this, and is a drone needed at all?
decisions.answer: Not for the papers' demo objects: a 2 m tower or 18 cm cylinder is faster and more accurate on a gantry or robot arm. Drones were chosen to prove aerial AM is possible.
decisions.rule: Use drones only if at least one holds: bigger than any machine envelope, at height or hard to reach, ground congested, or scaffolding would grow with span. Otherwise use a ground method.

decisions.title: Geometry envelope
decisions.question: Does the form fit what the chosen method can build?
decisions.answer: Keep to forms that slice into horizontal contour layers with thin single walls and no unsupported overhangs. Only single-wall cylinders were printed; domes and parabolic forms were virtual or simulated.
decisions.rule: Reject a version that can't be sliced into horizontal contours or has an overhang the layers can't step out to. Inclines beyond a gentle step need the stability strategy (DD06).

decisions.title: Material
decisions.question: Which material meets strength, weight and curing needs?
decisions.answer: Foam (~30 kg/m³) is light, fast and good for form studies and insulation, but expands unevenly and isn't structural. Cement mixes (~1741–1793 kg/m³ fresh, ~25 MPa target at 28 days) are heavier and slower, with 202 mL per trip. Mix No.1 holds shape best; No.4 flows best.
decisions.rule: Foam for scale and form tests. Cement for thin shells that must harden: Mix No.1 when layers slump, No.4 when the nozzle clogs. Either way, it must resist downwash and not set inside the extruder.

decisions.title: Tolerance
decisions.question: What deviation from the design is acceptable?
decisions.answer: ≤5 mm with the delta arm on cement, reported acceptable within UK building requirements. Foam without the arm reached 15 mm horizontal / 6 mm vertical max, and 2.27 cm median against the laser scan.
decisions.rule: Set ≤5 mm for cement with the arm, ~2–3 cm for foam. Anything tighter means another method.

decisions.title: Toolpath strategy
decisions.question: Fewer trips, or a smoother finish?
decisions.answer: Fewer trips. Per two layers the rounded Peano path is 5.85 m, hybrid 6.79 m, concentric 7.61 m, so Peano gets the most wall per cartridge. The paper used Peano for cement. Finish quality wasn't compared.
decisions.rule: Default to Peano while payload limits each trip. Consider concentric only when wall continuity matters more and payload allows (not tested).

decisions.title: Interim stability strategy
decisions.question: Adapt the design or the sequence, or add scaffolding?
decisions.answer: Change the design and sequence first. CAAM argues scaffolding scales badly (up to exponentially with span) and proposes a digital twin that checks every interim state, but shows this in simulation only.
decisions.rule: Vertical walls need neither. For inclines, run an interim stability check on the twin for each stage and adapt geometry or sequence. Add local scaffolding only where the check fails and the span is small.

decisions.title: Structural role
decisions.question: Is the printed part load-bearing, enclosure or formwork?
decisions.answer: Enclosure, formwork, insulation or repair, not load-bearing. Printed materials don't yet match reinforced concrete or steel. Reinforcement and structural design for aerial AM are open problems.
decisions.rule: Load-bearing only with reinforcement, structural analysis and code approval. Until then, non-structural.

decisions.title: Design freeze points
decisions.question: Which parts can still change once building starts?
decisions.answer: Freeze footprint, material, tolerance and structural role before printing. Keep upper geometry, toolpath offsets and sequence adaptable. Nature only adjusted layer height mid-build; CAAM proposes adapting design mid-build.
decisions.rule: Any change after the freeze goes through a buildability check and twin stability check, and is logged as a new design version.

decisions.title: Release next layer
decisions.question: Go, hold or adjust for the next layer?
decisions.answer: Go when the last layer is within tolerance, the layer below has cured, the stability check passes, conditions are within limits, and material and battery are ready. In the paper, ScanDrone scanned after every layer, the next path was offset, and a human supervised.
decisions.rule: All checks pass → go. One fails but is correctable by path offset → adjust. Cure, stability or conditions fail → hold. Cure and wind limits aren't in the papers: set them in a pilot.

decisions.title: Accept deviation
decisions.question: Is the as-built within tolerance, or correct the next layer?
decisions.answer: Correct the next layer. The paper measured mean top-layer height and offset the next trajectory, so drift didn't accumulate.
decisions.rule: Within tolerance → accept. Out of tolerance but fixable by offset → correct next layer. Same error several layers running → stop and review.

decisions.title: Mid-build design change
decisions.question: Change the design to match what was actually built?
decisions.answer: Small drift: no redesign, absorb it with offsets. Large accumulated drift: revise the upper layers to match the as-built, checked on the twin (CAAM's approach, simulated only).
decisions.rule: Redesign when the next layers can't meet tolerance or stability from the current as-built. Log the new version against the layers already built.

decisions.title: Fleet size
decisions.question: How many robots work this layer?
decisions.answer: Size the fleet to the contour. Robots self-retire as contours shrink; larger diameters gain more from added robots. The cement print used two drones in turn.
decisions.rule: Add robots while contour length allows safe spacing; retire them as the contour shrinks. With one-layer-per-load payloads, keep at least two so one prints while one refills.

decisions.title: Weather hold
decisions.question: Pause or continue in current conditions?
decisions.answer: Unknown: all tests were indoors. Wind affects path tracking and spray; temperature and water temperature affect curing.
decisions.rule: Set wind and temperature limits in an outdoor pilot. Pause above them; slow down near them. Don't print outside them.

decisions.title: Refill timing
decisions.question: When to refill material and swap batteries?
decisions.answer: Refill after every layer, as the paper did. One 202 mL cartridge is about one layer.
decisions.rule: Plan one load per layer and refill at layer end. Alternate two drones to keep the layer continuous, and stay inside the mix's open time.

decisions.title: Failure response
decisions.question: A robot failed or lost contact: reassign or stop?
decisions.answer: Reassign if the remaining robots can finish the layer within the mix's open time; otherwise stop at a clean layer boundary. The paper relies on redundancy for failures and comms loss.
decisions.rule: Remaining fleet can finish in open time → reassign. Can't → stop, let it cure, resume later.

decisions.title: Final acceptance
decisions.question: Does the finished build match the design?
decisions.answer: Accept when a laser scan of the as-built matches the design within tolerance. The paper validated the foam tower with a FARO scan (2.27 cm median).
decisions.rule: Scan vs design within tolerance across all layers → accept. Local exceedances → accept with notes or remediate.

decisions.title: Budget
decisions.question: Approve the budget for material, robot-hours and crew?
decisions.answer: The papers give no costs. Budget by trips (72 for a 2.05 m foam tower) × (material + battery cycles + crew time), plus scanning and supervision.
decisions.rule: Approve when trips, material volume and crew hours are estimated from the layer plan. Re-baseline if trips per layer change.

decisions.title: Schedule & weather windows
decisions.question: When does each phase run?
decisions.answer: Deposition time alone was 24 s per layer and 29 min total for the foam tower, and 2 h 13 min for 28 cement layers. Refills, scans, cure waits and weather add to that.
decisions.rule: Schedule = layers × (deposition + refill + scan + cure wait) inside forecast weather windows, plus buffer for holds.

decisions.title: Risk acceptance
decisions.question: Which risks does the project carry?
decisions.answer: Accept foam height drift (the scan loop corrects it). Mitigate downwash with fast-curing mixes and failures with spare robots. Avoid load-bearing use and untested outdoor conditions.
decisions.rule: Accept what a feedback loop corrects; mitigate what redundancy covers; avoid what no test has covered.

decisions.title: Scope change
decisions.question: Approve, defer or reject a change request?
decisions.answer: Before the freeze: allowed after a buildability check. After the freeze: only with a twin stability check and a new design version.
decisions.rule: Approve if it passes the checks and fits budget and schedule; defer if it waits on evidence; reject if it breaks a frozen item.

decisions.title: Staffing
decisions.question: Who supervises and supports each shift?
decisions.answer: At least one human supervisor (required in the paper) plus a refill and battery crew per shift. Refilling and battery swaps were manual.
decisions.rule: One supervisor and a ground crew sized to the fleet per shift, until refilling and charging are automated.

decisions.title: Permits & airspace
decisions.question: Are flight and building permits in place?
decisions.answer: Not covered by the papers. The review notes building codes haven't adapted to AM. Outdoor multi-drone flights need aviation approval wherever you build.
decisions.rule: Check local aviation rules for multi-drone operations and building-code acceptance before any outdoor build.

decisions.title: Material supply
decisions.question: Which supplier and batch for the mix?
decisions.answer: Cement mixes use Portland cement, pulverised fuel ash, xanthan gum, HEMC and plasticiser (some with foaming agent); the foam is two-part polyurethane. Short open times favour mixing at or near the site.
decisions.rule: Approve suppliers who meet the mix spec and can deliver within open-time limits.

decisions.title: Stakeholder sign-off
decisions.question: Do stakeholders approve passing this gate?
decisions.answer: Sign off at design gates 1–3, a safety gate before outdoor flights, and handover. Per-layer release is an internal gate, not a stakeholder one.
decisions.rule: Sign off when gate criteria are met and open risks are accepted in writing.
